title: Nuclear chemistry: decay and half-life
blurb: Predict the product of alpha, beta and gamma decay, work half-life problems by hand and tell fission from fusion.
question: A hospital tracer has a half-life of 6 hours. A 160 mg dose is made at 6:00 a.m. How much is left at 6:00 a.m. the next day, and what happens to the nucleus if the isotope decays by beta emission?

teach.body: Formally, radioactivity is the release of particles or energy by an unstable nucleus as it becomes more stable. In plain English: some nuclei have the wrong mix of protons and neutrons, so they throw something out. Because the number of protons can change, one element can turn into another (transmutation). Chemical reactions only move electrons, so they never change one element into another.

head: Emission
What it is
Mass no. / atomic no.
Stopped by
teach.caption: In beta decay a neutron turns into a proton, so the atomic number rises by 1. Alpha is the most ionizing but least penetrating; gamma is the reverse.

teach.body: Two totals must match on both sides: the mass numbers (top numbers) and the atomic numbers (bottom numbers, the charges). To find a product, subtract what was emitted. Alpha: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta: mass number unchanged, atomic number +1. Gamma: neither changes, the nucleus only loses energy. The new atomic number tells you the new element.

teach.caption: Protection from ionizing radiation: less time, more distance, more shielding.

teach.body: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay. It is fixed for each isotope and is not changed by heat, pressure or chemical form. After n half-lives, the fraction left is (1/2)ⁿ: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16. Work it by halving: 80 g with a 5-day half-life is 40, 20, 10 and 5 g after 5, 10, 15 and 20 days.

teach.caption: Decayed = 100% − remaining: after 2 half-lives, 25% remains and 75% has decayed.

teach.body: Keisha, a nuclear medicine technology applicant, reads that a tracer has a half-life of 6 hours. A 160 mg dose is prepared at 6:00 a.m. By 6:00 a.m. the next day, 24 hours have passed: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 half-lives. Halving four times: 160, 80, 40, 20, 10 mg. One-sixteenth remains; fifteen-sixteenths has decayed. Working backward also works: if 1/16 is left after 24 hours, the half-life is 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

rows.label: Needs
values: A neutron to start a chain

teach.caption: Both release energy from a tiny loss of mass (E = mc²). Fusion releases more energy per gram.

teach.text: Beta decay RAISES the atomic number by 1 (it does not lower it). Alpha is the LEAST penetrating; gamma has no mass and no charge. Half-life is the time for HALF to decay, not all: after 2 half-lives, 25% is left, not 0%. Read whether the item asks for the amount left or the amount decayed. The Sun uses fusion; power plants use fission.

items: Alpha: helium-4 nucleus, mass number −4, atomic number −2, stopped by paper.
Beta: electron from the nucleus, mass number unchanged, atomic number +1. Gamma: no change, most penetrating.
Balance nuclear equations by matching mass-number totals and atomic-number totals.
Half-life is constant; fraction left after n half-lives = (1/2)ⁿ. Decayed = 1 − remaining.
Fission splits heavy nuclei (power plants); fusion joins light nuclei (the Sun).

summary: You can now name alpha, beta and gamma radiation, predict the product of a decay by balancing mass and atomic numbers, and rank the emissions by penetrating power. You can also work half-life problems by halving and tell fission from fusion.

A.q: Which type of radiation is a high-energy photon with no mass and no charge?
A.why: Gamma rays are photons of electromagnetic energy, so they carry no mass and no charge.

whyNot.0: An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus with mass 4 and charge 2+.
whyNot.1: A beta particle is an electron, with a 1− charge.
whyNot.3: A positron is a positively charged particle with the mass of an electron.

A.q: A sample of an isotope has a half-life of 10 days. What fraction of the sample remains after 20 days?

whyNot.3: 1/20 divides by the number of days; each half-life halves the amount.

A.why: In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing enormous energy.

whyNot.0: Fission of uranium is used in nuclear power plants, not in the Sun.
whyNot.2: Helium-4 is stable and is the product of fusion, not a decaying fuel.
whyNot.3: Combustion is a chemical reaction; the Sun's energy is nuclear.

B.q: Polonium-210 (atomic number 84) emits an alpha particle. Which nucleus forms?
B.why: Alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4 (210 → 206) and the atomic number by 2 (84 → 82): lead-206.

whyNot.1: The mass number falls by 4, not 2: 210 − 4 = 206.
whyNot.2: Mass unchanged and atomic number +1 is beta decay, not alpha.
whyNot.3: The atomic number falls by 2, not 4: 84 − 2 = 82.

B.q: Which statement about half-life is correct?
options: Heating a sample shortens its half-life
It is the time for the whole sample to decay
It stays the same for a given isotope
Each half-life is shorter than the last
B.why: Half-life is a fixed property of each isotope; temperature, pressure and chemical form do not change it.

whyNot.0: Nuclear decay rates are not affected by temperature.
whyNot.1: Half-life is the time for HALF of the sample to decay.
whyNot.3: Every half-life is the same length; it is the amount that halves.

B.q: Sodium-24 (atomic number 11) undergoes beta decay. What are the mass number and atomic number of the product?
B.why: Beta decay keeps the mass number (24) and raises the atomic number by 1 (11 → 12): magnesium-24.

whyNot.0: Lowering the atomic number by 1 is positron emission, not beta decay.
whyNot.3: 25 and 11 describes gaining a neutron; beta decay keeps the mass number and raises the atomic number.

C.q: After 36 hours, 1/8 of a radioactive sample remains. What is the half-life of the isotope?

whyNot.0: 4.5 hours divides 36 by 8; 8 is the fraction's denominator, not the number of half-lives.
whyNot.2: 18 hours assumes 2 half-lives, which would leave 1/4.
whyNot.3: 9 hours assumes 4 half-lives, which would leave 1/16.

C.q: A 200 mg sample has a half-life of 3 days. How much of the sample has DECAYED after 9 days?

whyNot.0: 25 mg is the amount REMAINING after 3 half-lives, not the amount decayed.
whyNot.2: 150 mg has decayed after 2 half-lives (50 mg left); 9 days is 3 half-lives.
whyNot.3: 66.7 mg divides 200 by 3; each half-life halves what is left.

C.q: Which statement correctly compares alpha and gamma radiation?
options: Gamma is stopped by paper; alpha needs lead
Both change the atomic number of the nucleus
Alpha penetrates less; gamma needs thick lead
Alpha has no charge; gamma has a 2+ charge
C.why: Alpha particles are heavy and charged, so a sheet of paper or skin stops them. Gamma rays have no mass or charge and need thick lead or concrete.

whyNot.0: This reverses them: paper stops alpha, while gamma needs lead.
whyNot.1: Gamma emission leaves the atomic number unchanged; only alpha changes it here.
whyNot.3: This reverses the charges: alpha is 2+ and gamma is neutral.

reteach.title: Halving a pizza
reteach.question: Each time a timer rings, you eat exactly half of whatever pizza is left. How does that explain half-life?

blocks.body: Start with a whole pizza. First ring: half is left. Second ring: half of that half, a quarter. Third ring: an eighth. The time between rings never changes; that is the half-life. The pizza never vanishes all at once, and what you have eaten is the whole pizza minus what remains. Heating the oven does not make the timer ring sooner: half-life ignores temperature.

blocks.text: Read the question twice: 'how much remains' and 'how much has decayed' are different answers. After 3 half-lives, 1/8 remains and 7/8 has decayed.

explain.body: Alpha is a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons). Beta is an electron made when a neutron becomes a proton. Gamma is a photon of pure energy. Penetration rises from alpha to beta to gamma.

test.q: Which radiation is the least penetrating and is stopped by a sheet of paper?
test.why: Alpha particles are large and doubly charged, so they lose energy quickly and are stopped by paper or the outer skin.

whyNot.0: Gamma rays are the most penetrating and need thick lead or concrete.
whyNot.1: Beta particles pass through paper and are stopped by aluminum foil.
whyNot.2: X-rays are high-energy photons like gamma rays and pass through paper easily.

explain.body: The mass numbers on each side add up to the same total, and so do the atomic numbers. Subtract the emitted particle to find the product, then name the element from its new atomic number.

test.q: Thorium-234 (atomic number 90) undergoes beta decay. What is the atomic number of the product?
test.why: Beta decay turns a neutron into a proton: the atomic number rises by 1 (90 → 91) and the mass number stays 234.

whyNot.0: Lowering the atomic number by 1 is positron emission, not beta decay.
whyNot.1: Lowering it by 2 is alpha decay.
whyNot.3: An unchanged atomic number fits gamma emission.

explain.body: Divide the elapsed time by the half-life to get the number of half-lives, then halve that many times. Decayed = start − remaining.

test.q: An isotope has a half-life of 8 hours. How much of a 64 g sample remains after 24 hours?

whyNot.2: 21.3 g divides 64 by 3; each half-life halves the amount instead.

explain.body: Fission splits a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 after it absorbs a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons in a chain reaction. Fusion joins light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes into helium; it powers the Sun.

test.q: In a nuclear power plant, uranium-235 nuclei absorb neutrons and split. What is this process called?
test.why: Splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei is fission.

whyNot.0: Fusion joins light nuclei; it does not split heavy ones.
whyNot.2: Alpha decay releases a helium-4 nucleus without a neutron trigger and does not split the nucleus in two.
whyNot.3: Gamma emission releases energy without changing the nucleus's particles.
